messages.author: f4c1d095c7e7fa71
messages.subject: Analysis with uneven response lengths?
parts:
Hello all,

I have some data currently on animal diets. It's in the form of a list, with each element containing the masses of each predator's prey. So one element might have 100 masses, and another 1000. I'm trying to fit a Bayesian model to predict the prey mass distribution of a predator given the predator's mass and clade. Currently, I've been experimenting with estimating the mean and standard deviation of a predator's prey-mass distribution using the following model:

bf_Mean <- bf(preyMeans ~ (1 || Species_epithet/Genus/Order/Class) + (1 | Class)) + skew_normal()
bf_SD <- bf(preySD ~ log(as.numeric(PredMass)) + (1 || Species_epithet/Genus/Order/Class) + (1 | Class)) + student()

fit1 <- brm(bf_Mean + bf_SD + set_rescor(FALSE), data = Data, chains = 1, warmup = 2500, iter = 5000, cores = 3, set_prior("cauchy(0,2)", resp="preySD"))

I'm wondering first-and-foremost if there's anywhere to use the full preyList data instead of fitting just the summary statistics using brms, or do I need to build the model in stan? 

Secondly, I'm wondering if I've got the R-syntax for the nested model correct. Finally, I'm wondering if I've set set the priors correctly (specifically, the prior on the prey's standard deviation, which is the only one that shouldn't be normal).

Thank you for any help/advice!

--Jon

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Analysis with uneven response lengths?
parts:
This seems to call for the dis. ributional regression framework of brms. Assume you have data in long format (all observations of all species under each other) and that the response is approximately normal:Then I would try something like

bform <- bf(PreyMass ~ PredMass + (1 || Species_epithet/Genus/Order/Class) + (1 | Class),
                   sigma ~ PredMass + (1 || Species_epithet/Genus/Order/Class) + (1 | Class))
fit1 <- brm(bform, data = <long data>, family = gaussian())

Of course you can change the family if you feel the distribution is different.

See vignette("brms_distreg") for more details on the distributional regression approach of brms.

messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Analysis with uneven response lengths?
parts:
**Don't** use a model of the form

pprey ~ 1 + species + subclade + clade + (1 || species/subclade/clade)

as it trys to estimates effects of species etc. twice! This obviously won't end well.

I suggest you look at the coef() method for how to extract random effects coefficients.

2018-03-30 2:10 GMT+02:00 Jonathan Mitchell <jonsm...@gmail.com>:
I think I'm misunderstanding something fundamental about the brms syntax. I apologize if this question is covered in help files, but I can't quite seem to determine it.

Basically, in fitting a hierarchical distributional model, is it possible to extract the estimated location/scale/shape values for the group-level effects? Or do I have to include them as population level effects?

Below, I have greater detail, & a quick-and-dirty simulation and model.

What I'd like to do is compare the estimated mean/sd for clade with the true values. That is, something like (from the simulation below)

plot(CladePrime_means, <estimated mean for the clade from brms>)
plot(CladeSec_means, <estimated mean for subclade from brms>)
etc. etc.


# Simulate data
Nspecies <- 100
CladePrime_means <- runif(2, min=1, max=10)
CladePrime_sd <- abs(rstudent_t(2, 4))
names(CladePrime_sd) <- 1:2
names(CladePrime_means) <- 1:2

Parent_CladePrime <- sample(names(CladePrime_means), size=Nspecies / 10, replace=T)
CladeSec_means <- rnorm(Nspecies / 10, mean=0, sd=0.5)
CladeSec_means <- CladeSec_means + CladePrime_means[Parent_CladePrime]
CladeSec_sd <- runif(Nspecies / 10, min=0.01, max=0.2)
CladeSec_sd <- (CladePrime_sd[Parent_CladePrime]*CladeSec_sd ) + CladePrime_sd[Parent_CladePrime]
names(CladeSec_means) <- 1:(Nspecies / 10 )
names(CladeSec_sd) <- 1:(Nspecies / 10 )
names(Parent_CladePrime) <- names(CladeSec_means)

Parent_CladeSec <- sample(names(CladeSec_means), size=Nspecies, replace=T)
Species_means <- rnorm(Nspecies, mean=0, sd=0.1)
Species_means <- Species_means + CladeSec_means[Parent_CladeSec]
Species_sd <- runif(Nspecies, min=0.01, max=0.2)
Species_sd <- (CladeSec_sd[Parent_CladeSec]*Species_sd) + CladeSec_sd[Parent_CladeSec]

CladeSecVec <- as.factor(Parent_CladeSec)
CladePrimeVec <- as.factor(Parent_CladePrime[Parent_CladeSec])
SpeciesVec <- as.factor(1:Nspecies)
SizeVec <- rnorm(Nspecies, mean=5, sd=2)

for (i in 1:Nspecies) {
N <- sample(20:100, 1)
Data <- rnorm(N, Species_means[i], Species_sd[i])
pData <- Data - SizeVec[i]
Matrix <- data.frame(prey = Data, pprey = pData, logsize = rep(SizeVec[i], N), species = rep(SpeciesVec[i], N), subclade = rep(CladeSecVec[i], N), clade = rep(CladePrimeVec[i], N))
if (i == 1) {
dataMat <- Matrix
}
else if (i > 1) {
dataMat <- rbind(dataMat, Matrix)
}
}

### Model
bform <- bf(pprey ~ 1 + (1 || species/subclade/clade),
                   sigma ~ 1 + logsize + (1 + logsize || species/subclade/clade))

Priors <- get_prior(bform, data = dataMat)
Prior <- c(
prior(student_t(3, 0, 4), class=sd, coef="", group="species:subclade:clade"),
prior(student_t(3, 0, 4), class=sd, coef="", group="species:subclade"),
prior(student_t(3, 0, 4), class=sd, coef="", group="species"),
prior(normal(0,1), class=sd, coef="Intercept", group="species:subclade:clade"),
prior(normal(0,1), class=sd, coef="Intercept", group="species:subclade"),
prior(normal(0,1), class=sd, coef="Intercept", group="species")
)

fit1 <- brm(bform, data = dataMat, family = gaussian(), chains = 1, warmup = 500, iter = 1000, inits="0", control=list(max_treedepth = 20))

Or is it necessary to specify the model as something like:

bform <- bf(pprey ~ 1 + species + subclade + clade + (1 || species/subclade/clade),
                   sigma ~ 1 + logsize + species + subclade + clade + (1 + logsize || species/subclade/clade))

in order to estimate the marginal effect of clade membership on the resulting distribution?

I'm stuck on the syntax. I've been exploring coef() extensively. The problem is, the simulation produces a bimodal distribution (two gaussian distributions, with their means determined by the value of clade, and their variances as a function of species/subclade/clade means & variances)... 

Yet in in coef, the only items in the list are of the form x$`species`, x%`species:subclade`, x$`species:subclade:clade`. I'd assume that the third there represents the clade-specific portion of the interaction, yet despite high R2's and very-good looking PP checks, that third element is decidedly unimodal.

Essentially, I want a hierarchical model that estimates means and standard deviations for each (nested) level, yet I cannot figure out how to extract those for these data. I assume I'm missing something blindingly obvious, but I can't figure out what.

parts:
A few questions:

1. What exactly is bimodal?
2. With species/subclade/clade  you imply that clades are nested in subclades which are nested in species just like students are nested in classes are nested in schools. Is this what you intended?

If you study coef(...)$species, you see it is an array of 3 dimensions. The first indicates levels, the second indicates summary statistics and the 3rd indicates coefficients. In your model, the third dimension should be of length 3 with one coefficient (per species) for the mean (Intercept) and two for the residual SD sigma (namely sigma_Intercept and sigma_logsize).

                   sigma ~ PredMass + (1 || Species_epithet/Genus/Order/Class) + (1 | Class))
fit1 <- brm(bform, data = <long data>, family = gaussian())

Of course you can change the family if you feel the distribution is different.

See vignette("brms_distreg") for more details on the distributional regression approach of brms.
